links.comparator_used: Single-agent control condition (one LLM making and checking the decision) vs a nine-agent role-differentiated pipeline (assessment, allocation, independent audit)
links.outcome: Rate of biased outcomes in synthetic disaster-triage resource allocation (paired cases differing by one demographic attribute)
links.effect: 6.9% vs. 6.1% biased outcomes, p = 0.498 (192 episodes, 2,304 resolved case pairs, GPT-4o-mini)
links.quote: We find no measurable difference in how often biased outcomes occur between the two conditions (6.9% vs. 6.1%, p = 0.498).

links.comparator_used: Overloaded (capacity-constrained) auditor agent vs non-overloaded auditor agent within the multi-agent pipeline
links.outcome: Proportion of biased outcomes going undetected by the independent audit agent
links.effect: 30.0% of biased outcomes undetected overall; 43.8% when the auditor is overloaded vs 18.4% when it is not. Review coverage fell from 100.0% to 65.6% under load (p < 0.001), while judgment on reviewed cases was 81.6% vs 85.7% (p = 1.000). Risk-ordered audit queue restored coverage from 65.6% to 91.7% (p = 0.028).
links.tradeoff: Audit effectiveness depends on capacity: under load, cases are not reviewed at all (coverage loss), so bias goes undetected; the audit agent did not reduce the bias rate itself.
links.quote: We do find a large and significant effect of audit capacity on whether bias is caught: 30.0% of biased outcomes go entirely undetected, rising to 43.8% when the auditor is overloaded and falling to 18.4% when it is not.

design_hint: multi-agent audit pipeline and risk-prioritized audit queuing
